title: Who may implement what?
subtitle: The orphan rule: click any cell
intro: Each cell is an impl Trait for Type written in your crate. Select one to see why the compiler accepts or rejects it.

cells.point-describe: Both the trait and the type are yours. Anything goes.
cells.point-display: The trait is foreign but Point is local, so your crate is the only place this impl can ever live. This is how you make your own types printable with {}.
cells.point-iterator: Allowed for the same reason: the type is local. You would provide type Item and fn next, and every iterator adapter becomes available on Point.
cells.i32-describe: A local trait can be implemented for foreign types. This is the extension trait pattern: you add methods to i32, visible wherever your trait is in scope.
cells.i32-display: Both Display and i32 belong to std, which already has this impl. If your crate could add one, two crates could add conflicting ones: coherence forbids it.
cells.i32-iterator: Foreign trait, foreign type. Only std could write this impl. Wrap the value in a newtype (struct Counter(i32);) to implement it yourself.
cells.vecT-describe: A blanket impl over a foreign generic type is fine when the trait is local: impl<T> Describe for Vec<T>.
cells.vecT-display: Vec and Display are both foreign. std deliberately leaves this out because there is no single right way to display a list.
cells.vecT-iterator: Foreign trait, foreign type. Note that Vec is not an iterator itself, it implements IntoIterator instead.
cells.vecPoint-describe: Local trait: allowed, and more specific than a blanket impl over Vec<T> (you cannot have both, they would overlap).
cells.vecPoint-display: Surprising but rejected: a local type inside a foreign one does not make Vec<Point> local. Use a newtype: struct Points(Vec<Point>);
cells.vecPoint-iterator: Rejected for the same reason. A newtype around the vector is again the escape hatch.
